props.title: Glen or Glenda
props.initialSlug: Ed Wood's bizarre plea for transgender acceptance

sections.content: Glen or Glenda (1953) stands as Ed Wood's most personal and groundbreaking film, tackling transgender identity and cross-dressing decades before mainstream cinema dared approach these themes. Wood himself stars as Glen/Glenda under the pseudonym Daniel Davis, bringing raw authenticity to the semi-autobiographical role. While infamously featuring Bela Lugosi's cryptic narration and surreal dream sequences with buffalo stampedes, the film's earnest plea for tolerance was revolutionary for 1953. It shares DNA with later transgender cinema like The World According to Garp (1982) and Dog Day Afternoon (1975), which also challenged gender norms, albeit with bigger budgets.

sections.content: Wood's guerrilla filmmaking approach influenced generations of outsider artists, from John Waters to the Kuchar brothers. While Plan 9 from Outer Space (1959) gets labeled Wood's signature "worst film," Glen or Glenda reveals his true artistic soul. The film's structure - mixing documentary-style narration, dramatic reenactments, and fever-dream sequences - created a template for later experimental LGBTQ cinema like Pink Narcissus (1971) and Flaming Creatures (1963).

Modern transgender cinema like Boys Don't Cry (1999) and A Fantastic Woman (2017) builds on Wood's foundational work, though with more polished execution. Glen or Glenda's raw emotional honesty about gender identity struggles resonates through Hedwig and the Angry Inch (2001) and Tangerine (2015). Wood's use of documentary techniques to normalize transgender experiences predates similar approaches in Paris Is Burning (1990) and The Queen (1968). SUBHEAD: Impact on Independent Cinema

sections.content: Wood's DIY aesthetic and personal storytelling influenced the New Queer Cinema movement of the 1990s. Films like My Own Private Idaho (1991) and The Living End (1992) echo Wood's blend of surrealism and social commentary. Even mainstream productions like The Danish Girl (2015) and Dallas Buyers Club (2013) owe a debt to Wood's pioneering representation of gender-nonconforming characters.
